messages.subject: Estimate Absolute Number of Encounters
messages.subject_clean: Estimate Absolute Number of Encounters
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I'm trying to estimate the total number of encounters between two animals during a shared observation period. I used the rates() function on their UDs to calculate pairwise encounter probabilities in units of 1/m^2. My initial idea was to multiply this by the intersection area between the UDs, but I'm uncertain if that's the correct approach.

According to the encounter statistics documentation (https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/encounter.html), it mentions that these values "must be multiplied by the square encounter radius (in meters) to obtain other values." This seems promising, but I'm not entirely sure. Specifically, I have two questions:

1) Will multiplying by the square encounter radius yield the absolute number of encounters in the observation period, and if so, how do I calculate this radius?

2) If this is not the correct method, do you have an alternative approach?

Thank you,
Odd

messages.subject: Re: Estimate Absolute Number of Encounters
messages.subject_clean: Estimate Absolute Number of Encounters
messages.body_plain:
Hi Odd,

I just recently updated that function to the predicted encounter probability divided by the square encounter radius ( and changed the name to encounter(), with the CDE function name changed to cde() ). The immediate output is the expected proportion of time predicted to include 1-meter encounters, and if you multiply by 100^2 then you get the expected proportion of time predicted to include 100-meter encounters. The distance you plug in just needs to be much smaller than the home-range scales for the approximations used.

On the other hand, if you want the observed proportion of times, then you want the distances() function. But if the encounter probability is low, then you can often observe nothing.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: ctmm::meta() with scaled Homerange-sizes
messages.subject_clean: ctmm::meta() with scaled Homerange-sizes
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am comparing AKDE sizes using ctmm::meta(). I have two different species and two different treatments. I would like to show that the treatment is the more important predictor of homerange size, although both species slightly differ in their homerange sizes (not significant, and not meaningful). What I did until here:

1) compared both species without considering treatment
2) compared only treatments
3) compared each species with both treatments

 However, I would like to bring this together and end up with only one estimate of the effect size, how the treatment affects homerange size. I was thinking about scaling (scale()) the homerange sizes for each group and then applying the meta-analysis on these scaled hr estimates. Does that make any sense? I struggle to get my head around the functions within the meta-function, so if anyone has an idea of how to implement it, I would be very happy to learn from you.

Thanks in advance,

Marius

messages.subject: Trouble interpreting null model approach for artefactual periodicity test
messages.subject_clean: Trouble interpreting null model approach for artefactual periodicity test
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I'm interested in assessing space use and resource selection of Arctic and red foxes during the breeding season, and I have a data set containing GPS data collected at a frequency of 1 fix/15 minutes between April - August 2023. I think it'd be really interesting to look at periodic patterns of space use, but I'm a little concerned that my sampling schedule produces artefactual periodicity. The sampling schedule rotates on a 4-day cycle, collecting 1 fix/15 min for 6 hours each day so that in 4 days all 24 hours are covered (i.e., day 1 hours = 000-0600, day 2 hours = 0600-1200, day 3 hours = 1200-1800, day 4 hours = 1800-2400).

When I did a visual assessment of variograms/periodograms for two foxes, Randy and Woody, I had trouble interpreting what I was seeing. It appears Woody exhibits range residency from the variogram, although Randy is a different story. I'm not sure why the best fitting model for Randy varies so much from the variogram, but I don't suspect Randy is resident. To give some background on Randy's movements, it appears Randy was captured and collared during either an exploratory movement or a dispersal, as the next two days after capture it moves and settles ~25 km from the capture location. It stays in this area for ~ 1 month and then disperses northwest of the study area, where it appears to have remained and established a home range. I'm not sure why the variogram doesn't reflect that pattern.

The sampling schedule periodograms (red) seem very similar to Woody and Randy's periodograms (black), so I suspected this might be indicative of artefactual periodicity. I attempted to use the code in Additional File 3 from Péron et al. (2016) <https://doi.org/10.1186/s40462-016-0084-7>, but I got the same output for both foxes when I ran the period.test function:

> period.test(Woody, Woody.OUF, n = 100) # period (days) = 14745600/(86400) = 170, p = 0
> period.test(Randy, Randy.OUF, n = 100) # period (days) = 14745600/(86400) = 170, p = 0

Here is a link to the R script and data I used to generate all models, figures, and tests: https://github.com/gamblinh/FoxData_Periodicity

Is it a problem with my code? Am I overlooking some glaring issue in the model diagnostics?

Also, as more of a basic question, how exactly does one interpret a periodogram? I tried following the Péron et al. (2016) <https://doi.org/10.1186/s40462-016-0084-7> and the Calabrese et al. (2016) <https://doi-org.uml.idm.oclc.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12559> paper (and associated appendices, such as Appendix C), and I'm still struggling to interpret the graph. I understand vertical lines and peaks indicate the period of repeated space use, but how exactly do I interpret the graph? What are those little black ticks on the x-axis? How do I tease out the exact hour/day/month that the periodic pattern occurs? My apologies for this basic question.

Thank you so much for your help!

Woody variogram with OUF model overlayed

Woody periodogram

Randy variogram with OUF model overlayed

Randy periodogram

messages.subject_clean: Trouble interpreting null model approach for artefactual periodicity test
messages.body_plain:
Hi Holly,

Since that paper was published, ctmm.select() was updated with an appropriate model selection criterion for that model (based on AIC/BIC + MSPE). Presently, you should just be able to call ctmm.select() and go with the output of that.

The x-axis of the variogram is "time lag" between two times and not absolute time. It will not reflect the schedule over which the data were collected, but here Randy's variogram seems to indicate resident phase(s) of the data about ~1 week long, within a much larger dispersal range on a seasonal scale, while Woody's variogram is mostly resident day-to-day, but slightly shifted over the seasonal scale.

If the data are evenly sampled, then the peaks of the periodogram correspond to the periods and harmonics (integer fractions of the period) of repeating space use. The tick marks correspond to meaningful periods (e.g., a day) and their potential harmonics (e.g., 1/2 a day, 1/3 a day, 1/4 a day, ...). I will update the help file with this information. Here you have peaks corresponding to the 4-day, 1-day and 6-hr scheduling, so you can't really see anything in the periodogram of the data (black) that isn't in the periodogram of the schedule (red).

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Cris,

Thank you! Also, I noticed a new vignette on pairwise interactions (https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/interactions.html) - this is very helpful.

I have two questions after reviewing the vignette:

1)  How well do methods like distance(), proximity(), and encounter() perform when comparing animals sampled non-simultaneously? In my case, I am interested in studying interactions among 10 capuchin groups, each sampled over the same sampling window (over a calendar year), but not simultaneously. I am working with handheld GPS data (collected by human observers following habituated groups), therefore the data could only be collected on one group at a time. Does it still make sense to use these methods? Are the continuous-time movement models capable of accurately predicting interactions during unsampled times (gaps in data)?

2) Also, with regards to a slightly different dataset, would you recommend these methods when the data is independent (~1 location per day)?

Thanks,
Odd

Hi Odd,
Yes and you get predictions with confidence intervals in the gaps. So, at times that are not well resolved, you will have larger uncertainties.
The confidence intervals will just widen out and you will get back nothing but uncertainty. It won't hurt anything, but you won't get anything.
Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Thank you so much for your explanation! I was worried the peaks were more related to the sampling schedule than true periodicity. If there is artefactual periodicity from the schedule, is there an alternative way to get at the question of periodic patterns of space use?

I did have one follow-up question in regard to null hypothesis testing to confirm artefactual periodicity. In my original code I had used the ctmm.select() function, which indicated OUF was the best model for both foxes. The models in the variograms are from the ctmm.select() function. When I ran the period.test function with the fitted OUF models, the values for Woody and Randy were identical and it returned P = 0, which seems suspicious considering the periodograms seem to indicate artefactual periodicity. I've pasted a shortened version of the code below for an example (full code and data available at https://github.com/gamblinh/FoxData_Periodicity):

# RF Woody #

#Calculate the variogram

Woody.vg<-variogram(Woody)

plot(Woody.vg)

#Calculate the periodogram

Woody.pg <- periodogram(Woody)

plot(Woody.pg, diagnostic = TRUE)

#Use the sliders provided by variogram.fit to specify starting values.

variogram.fit(Woody.vg)

#save the parameters in the manipulator window to GUESS

#Automatically fit the range-resident models via maximum likelihood

Woody.fit.mods<-ctmm.select(Woody,CTMM=GUESS, verbose=TRUE)

summary(Woody.fit.mods)

# OUF Anisotropic is top model for Woody

Woody.OUF<-Woody.fit.mods[[1]]

summary(Woody.OUF)

plot(Woody.vg, CTMM = Woody.OUF)

# Note that AF Randy OUF calculated using similar code to Woody

############################################################

# Function from Appendix

############################################################

period.test=function(data,model,period=NULL,n=100,deltat=60,...) {

  # initiate output vector

  RES=NULL

  # compute periodogram of the true data

  per=periodogram(data,...)

  # set period of interest at the periodogram peak if not provided by user

  if(is.null(period)) period=1/per$f[which.max(per$LSP)]

  else period=period[1]

  # MC loop

  for (k in 1:n) {

    # simulate dataset using model provided by user and time grid from the true data

    s=simulate(object=model,t=data$t-data$t[1])

    # compute periodogram of the simulated dataset

    s.per=periodogram(s,...)

    # compute whether simulated value is higher than true value

    RES=c(RES, max(s.per$LSP[abs(1/s.per$f - period)<=deltat])<

            max(per$LSP[abs(1/per$f - period)<=deltat]) )

  }

  return(list(period=period,P.value=1-sum(RES)/sum(!is.na <http://is.na>(RES))))

}

####################################################################

#returns a list with two items: tested period in seconds and P-value of that period

period.test(Woody, Woody.OUF, n = 1000) # period (days) = 14745600/(3600*24) = 170,  p = 0

period.test(Randy, Randy.OUF, n = 1000) # period(days) = 14745600/(3600*24) = 170, p = 0

On Tuesday, October 3, 2023 at 8:06:40 PM UTC-5 Christen Fleming wrote:
> Hi Holly,
>
> Since that paper was published, ctmm.select() was updated with an appropriate model selection criterion for that model (based on AIC/BIC + MSPE). Presently, you should just be able to call ctmm.select() and go with the output of that.
>
> The x-axis of the variogram is "time lag" between two times and not absolute time. It will not reflect the schedule over which the data were collected, but here Randy's variogram seems to indicate resident phase(s) of the data about ~1 week long, within a much larger dispersal range on a seasonal scale, while Woody's variogram is mostly resident day-to-day, but slightly shifted over the seasonal scale.
>
> If the data are evenly sampled, then the peaks of the periodogram correspond to the periods and harmonics (integer fractions of the period) of repeating space use. The tick marks correspond to meaningful periods (e.g., a day) and their potential harmonics (e.g., 1/2 a day, 1/3 a day, 1/4 a day, ...). I will update the help file with this information. Here you have peaks corresponding to the 4-day, 1-day and 6-hr scheduling, so you can't really see anything in the periodogram of the data (black) that isn't in the periodogram of the schedule (red).
>
> Best,
> Chris
>
> On Tuesday, October 3, 2023 at 3:19:51 PM UTC-4 Holly Gamblin wrote:
> > Hi there,
> >
> > I'm interested in assessing space use and resource selection of Arctic and red foxes during the breeding season, and I have a data set containing GPS data collected at a frequency of 1 fix/15 minutes between April - August 2023. I think it'd be really interesting to look at periodic patterns of space use, but I'm a little concerned that my sampling schedule produces artefactual periodicity. The sampling schedule rotates on a 4-day cycle, collecting 1 fix/15 min for 6 hours each day so that in 4 days all 24 hours are covered (i.e., day 1 hours = 000-0600, day 2 hours = 0600-1200, day 3 hours = 1200-1800, day 4 hours = 1800-2400).
> >
> > When I did a visual assessment of variograms/periodograms for two foxes, Randy and Woody, I had trouble interpreting what I was seeing. It appears Woody exhibits range residency from the variogram, although Randy is a different story. I'm not sure why the best fitting model for Randy varies so much from the variogram, but I don't suspect Randy is resident. To give some background on Randy's movements, it appears Randy was captured and collared during either an exploratory movement or a dispersal, as the next two days after capture it moves and settles ~25 km from the capture location. It stays in this area for ~ 1 month and then disperses northwest of the study area, where it appears to have remained and established a home range. I'm not sure why the variogram doesn't reflect that pattern.
> >
> > The sampling schedule periodograms (red) seem very similar to Woody and Randy's periodograms (black), so I suspected this might be indicative of artefactual periodicity. I attempted to use the code in Additional File 3 from Péron et al. (2016) <https://doi.org/10.1186/s40462-016-0084-7>, but I got the same output for both foxes when I ran the period.test function:
> >
> > > period.test(Woody, Woody.OUF, n = 100) # period (days) = 14745600/(86400) = 170, p = 0
> > > period.test(Randy, Randy.OUF, n = 100) # period (days) = 14745600/(86400) = 170, p = 0
> >
> > Here is a link to the R script and data I used to generate all models, figures, and tests: https://github.com/gamblinh/FoxData_Periodicity
> >
> > Is it a problem with my code? Am I overlooking some glaring issue in the model diagnostics?
> >
> > Also, as more of a basic question, how exactly does one interpret a periodogram? I tried following the Péron et al. (2016) <https://doi.org/10.1186/s40462-016-0084-7> and the Calabrese et al. (2016) <https://doi-org.uml.idm.oclc.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12559> paper (and associated appendices, such as Appendix C), and I'm still struggling to interpret the graph. I understand vertical lines and peaks indicate the period of repeated space use, but how exactly do I interpret the graph? What are those little black ticks on the x-axis? How do I tease out the exact hour/day/month that the periodic pattern occurs? My apologies for this basic question.
> >
> > Thank you so much for your help!
> >
> > Woody variogram with OUF model overlayed
> >
> > Woody periodogram
> >
> > Randy variogram with OUF model overlayed
> >
> > Randy periodogram

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Follow up to my overlapping home ranges question!

I found that many of my cats constrict or expand their home range seasonally, but don't actually shift very far. So a low overlap percentage doesn't necessarily tell me that they moved to a new area, just that their two home ranges overlap minimally. Attached plot show 4 years of winter - to - summer overlap comparisons for the same cat. Only in 2023 does it look like she actually shifted her range. However, if I just use a cutoff of the overlap value to make decisions about shifts, I would have wrongly classified 2022 as a shift too.

My next thought was that I should look at mean centroid shifts between home ranges as part of the decision process to classify if a cat shifted vs expanded/constricted (if their overlap is small).

I used ctmm::distance on the FITS objects for each site (as we talked about above), like this:
books_distances <- ctmm::distance(FITS.books, method="Euclidean",  sqrt=TRUE)

However, all the values are absolutely massive. I tested both  sqrt=TRUE and  sqrt=FALSE, which gave me the same values. So I am not sure if the output units for this are in meters or sq meters or something completely different. After cleaning up the resulting matrices so I only had pairwise comparisons between the same individuals's various seasons, I divided the values by 1e+6 (assuming it was in sq m) to get sq km.
But comparing the overlap values and the distance results make no sense. For example, one cat (CA07) has an overlap of 93.6% between her Winter 2019 and Summer 2019. However, the distance given for that same pairwise comparison is 2.219973e+10, which (if is supposed to be meters), would be 22,199.73 sq km. That is clearly not correct.

I think this means I did something wrong in fitting the distance() function, so I was hoping you could see a glaring issue that I missed :D
Thanks for all your help!!

Kristin

DOF[area] = 3.33576466709752e-13." This seems similar to the issue I had with the other dataset with 2 individuals, where you explained that the results may not be useful because of large CIs. Subsequently, I was unable to run either the pkde() or mean(), and (just for fun) overlap(). The error after pkde() and mean() was: "Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...) : no slot of name "CTMM" for this object of class "ctmm"." For overlap(), I got this error: "Error in dr[1, ] : incorrect number of dimensions"

> > Hi Connie,
> >
> > Thanks for the example data. I noticed that some numerical gradient code wasn't doing a good job in that example and upgraded that code to analytic formulas, which I tested to work much better. This update is on Github now, however:
> >
> > The PKDE estimate does not come out to be good with these two individuals because you get variance collapse in the population model estimates, in that the uncertainty in the individual parameter estimates is large enough to explain all of the variation in the data.
> >
> > In situations like this, assuming that you have to report something, I would run pkde() and mean() on the UDs and then take the larger of the two estimates. mean() does not extrapolate from the sample to the population like pkde() does, but with really weak data (like only 2 points here) pkde() can suffer more from variance collapse.
> >
> > Best,
> > Chris
> >
> > On Monday, September 25, 2023 at 9:22:05 PM UTC-4 Connie Kot wrote:
> > > Hi Chris,
> > > Thanks for looking into this! In the past, we have resorted to calculating the mean KDE with the knowledge that this is not ideal. After looking at the results from the pkde() function, it seemed like the resulting UDs were in between UDs using the IID model fit and UDs calculated as the mean UDs (aKDEs). > > > >
> > > > I don't think its safe to run pkde() on just two individuals. That would be like running akde() on two locations. I can work on coding that to be more robust, but I would never trust that output.

> > > > > > > The documentation is using ctmm.fit() in specific cases where I know that is safe to do (for computational speed), but also informing you not to do that on your data (unless you know better).
> > > > > > > If you are able to segment your data into resident segments and dispersal segments, then I would recommend estimating separate ranges for each, and reporting them separately. Also IIRC, I believe you were using mean() when you probably want to be using pkde(), but the latter is more sensitive to data quality issues. The former is the mean of the sample, while the latter is the extrapolated population range.
> > > > > > > When you have a small effective sample size (unless its from location error) then the AKDE is underestimated, but you still get appropriately wide confidence intervals. Switching to IID KDE is exacerbating that negative bias.
> > > > > > > Best,

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

First, I'd like to thank everyone for the great discussions I have been reading in this group! They have been very enlightening.

I am currently fitting akdes to highly irregularly sampled VHF data from 16 territorial forest songbirds that we tracked this summer. I have had no trouble producing UDs on 15 of the 16 birds, but the function consistently fails for the last bird, giving me the following error:

Warning: Fit object returned. DOF[area] = 4.85145214203012e-07Error in akde(data[SUB], CTMM[SUB], VMM = VMM[SUB], R = R, SP = SP, SP.in = SP.in, : Data not in single coordinate system.

I have gone through the csv line-by-line for this bird and found no erroneous coordinates. The entire csv is in decimal degrees. Does anyone have any idea what may be causing this issue?

Thanks,
Tyler

Hi Chris,

Thanks! Hope you are doing well!

I have a few 'weird' movement model fits which I am trying to fix. Is segmenting the data the only option usually? For example, see Dog 27 (1st is default zoomed, 2nd 100% zoomed out, 3rd is the selected movement model fit, 4th is the home range contour).

I am afraid of segmenting the data further because some of the dogs in a few seasons have limited data (few days). Let me know what would you suggest to do in such cases. Best,
Soham Mehta

Hello Chris,

Ah, that would make sense! Although most displayed range residency behavior, a few of the birds definitely displayed non-stationary behavior during different periods of the breeding cycle (e.g., slightly shifting ranges a couple hundred meters during second nesting attempts or the post-fledging and post-breeding periods). I planned to split up the locations by time of season or behavior at some point, but I was trying to force the full-season AKDEs for comparison's/exploration's sake and for practice while I find my way around ctmm.

Strangely, the projection() function indicates that both the data and fit objects have the same reference coordinates and projections (wgs84).

I had a very irregular sampling interval. At its core, I did two-minute burst sampling (see Barg et al. 2005) for 30 minutes every other day, with sessions alternating between morning and afternoon to help account for any temporal variation in space use. However, depending on the bird's behavior, the sampling interval ranged between as little as two minutes to as long as 30 minutes during the session window (sometimes we were only able to get a single location on a bird during the session). Additionally, I wasn't always able to track each bird every other day due to logistics and equipment malfunctions, especially early and late in the season. As a result, my variograms are quite messy (see below for the variogram for this particular bird), although I am sure there is an easy way to clean them up with the dt argument.

Best,
Tyler

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kristin,

In your script you have sqrt=FALSE, which will output square meters. Square rooted and dividing by 1000, I get point estimates ranging between 0-15km, which matches with their plots.
Setting sqrt=TRUE for output in meters and dividing by 1000, I get point estimates also ranging between 0-15km (slightly different values because of debiasing).

If you are getting something very different after updating, the Github installer probably failed to overwrite the old files. I would remove the package, restart R, and then re-install the package.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject_clean: "Data not in the same coordinate system"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tyler,

You are running ctmm.select() with verbose=TRUE, which returns a list of all candidate models. Then you are feeding the whole list to akde() with just one tracking dataset. There needs to be one (best) model per tracking dataset.
I will improve the error message.

Best,
Chris

At its core, I did two-minute burst sampling (see Barg et al. 2005) for 30 minutes every other day, with sessions alternating between morning and afternoon to help account for any temporal variation in space use. However, depending on the bird's behavior, the sampling interval ranged between as little as two minutes to as long as 30 minutes during the session window (sometimes we were only able to get a single location on a bird during the session). Additionally, I wasn't always able to track each bird every other day due to logistics and equipment malfunctions, especially early and late in the season. , , est

[2,] 1569701596          0   38264192   81861250  137041451 1202632905

However, if I take the sqrt of the resulting values and then divide by 1000, they make much more sense! I don't understand why the sqrt argument doesn't change the value estimation, but, if we assume the output is coming in square meters, then the numbers make more sense.

Thanks for your help,
Kristin

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kristin,

I can only suspect that there is a file locking issue happening, and that you need to delete the package, shutdown R, go into your package directory and make sure the ctmm folder is deleted, reboot your computer, startup R in a new workspace, and then re-install ctmm. Alternatively, you could try a different computer to make sure there's not something weird in your script causing this.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Range Residency in a Forest Bird with Variable Space Use
messages.subject_clean: Range Residency in a Forest Bird with Variable Space Use
messages.body_plain:
Hello group,

I don't mean to overly belabor the topic, but I was wondering about the range residency status of a subset of forest birds that I tracked via traditional VHF this past summer. Most of the birds demonstrated bounded home ranges throughout the breeding season with the variograms reaching obvious asymptotes, while others have variograms that are a bit questionable. Specifically, these birds had space use that changed slightly during different periods of the season, whereas the other birds had home ranges that remained static during the same time periods. As expected, the variograms for these birds are not typical, although for one of the birds with the least static whole-season space use (see discussion below), an asymptote does seem apparent. I am trying to get a handle on whether a full season analysis may be possible and appropriate with these birds, and if a mean breeding season home range size would be usable to inform other aspects of the study and analysis (e.g., I want to use the mean home range size to create a biologically meaningful buffer distance in which to summarize habitat covariates for point-counts conducted on the same study sites). Below, I share the questionable variograms and briefly discuss each bird's space use.

Note: When I refer to "movements", these are often only on the scale of a few hundred meters.

Bird 1

I was able to track this bird almost throughout the entire breeding season. At the beginning of the season, it had fairly static space use and was restricted to a small area, but during the post-fledging period its area of space use expanded greatly, and it was often found a few hundred meters from the area of original use. Then, during the post-breeding period, it briefly returned to its original area of use before settling in an area not too far from its original location. Despite this variable space use, however, the variogram seems rather stable.

Bird 2

This bird had a very similar space use history to bird 1, with it occupying a fairly static area for much of the season, briefly moving away from this area during the post-fledging period, and then returning to the original location during the post-breeding period. However, rather the apparent asymptote of the first bird, this one has a distinct bell shape.

Bird 3

This bird also has a bell-shaped curve. It had settled in one area for some time, moved to an adjacent area for what I suspect to be its first nesting attempt, and then moved back to the original location for the rest of the season, where we located an active nest.

Bird 4

Despite what seemed like fairly stable space use, this bird has a distinctly rising tail at the end of the variogram. I know the end of variograms can typically be discounted, but the rising pattern also seems to be a signature of variograms indicating non-range resident behavior, which is why I want someone with more skilled eyes to take a look at it for me.

Bird 5

Same story as bird #4, although it did have a couple tracking sessions that were located somewhat farther from its area of core use than normal.

Bird 6

Despite having an asymptote, this bird did slightly shift its area of core use during its second nesting attempt, although it was closer to its initial core use area than some of the movements displayed by the other birds discussed above.

Thanks in advance for any guidance you all can provide!

Best,
Tyler

Hi Tyler,

Just from the variograms, 1,4,5,6 don't appear significantly off, though you can use CI="Gauss" for better variogram CIs that will be narrower after the asymptote.
2 is intermediate and 3 is significantly and substantially off (the white space between the empirical and theoretical CIs). These variograms do match up to the behavior you describe.
I agree that 4,5,6 look like they might be increasing, but variogram errors are autocorrelated, so you can't necessarily ascribe a trend to that, as its within the expected range of errors.

Best,
Chris

> > I don't mean to overly belabor the topic, but I was wondering about the range residency status of a subset of forest birds that I tracked via traditional VHF this past summer. Most of the birds demonstrated bounded home ranges throughout the breeding season with the variograms reaching obvious asymptotes, while others have variograms that are a bit questionable. Specifically, these birds had space use that changed slightly during different periods of the season, whereas the other birds had home ranges that remained static during the same time periods. As expected, the variograms for these birds are not typical, although for one of the birds with the least static whole-season space use (see discussion below), an asymptote does seem apparent. I am trying to get a handle on whether a full season analysis may be possible and appropriate with these birds, and if a mean breeding season home range size would be usable to inform other aspects of the study and analysis (e.g., I want to use the mean home range size to create a biologically meaningful buffer distance in which to summarize habitat covariates for point-counts conducted on the same study sites). Below, I share the questionable variograms and briefly discuss each bird's space use.
> >
> > Note: When I refer to "movements", these are often only on the scale of a few hundred meters.
> >
> > Bird 1
> >
> > I was able to track this bird almost throughout the entire breeding season. At the beginning of the season, it had fairly static space use and was restricted to a small area, but during the post-fledging period its area of space use expanded greatly, and it was often found a few hundred meters from the area of original use. Then, during the post-breeding period, it briefly returned to its original area of use before settling in an area not too far from its original location. Despite this variable space use, however, the variogram seems rather stable.
> >
> > Bird 2
> >
> > This bird had a very similar space use history to bird 1, with it occupying a fairly static area for much of the season, briefly moving away from this area during the post-fledging period, and then returning to the original location during the post-breeding period. However, rather the apparent asymptote of the first bird, this one has a distinct bell shape.
> >
> > Bird 3
> >
> >
> > This bird also has a bell-shaped curve. It had settled in one area for some time, moved to an adjacent area for what I suspect to be its first nesting attempt, and then moved back to the original location for the rest of the season, where we located an active nest.
> >
> > Bird 4
> >
> > Despite what seemed like fairly stable space use, this bird has a distinctly rising tail at the end of the variogram. I know the end of variograms can typically be discounted, but the rising pattern also seems to be a signature of variograms indicating non-range resident behavior, which is why I want someone with more skilled eyes to take a look at it for me.
> >
> > Bird 5
> >
> > Same story as bird #4, although it did have a couple tracking sessions that were located somewhat farther from its area of core use than normal.
> >
> > Bird 6
> >
> > Despite having an asymptote, this bird did slightly shift its area of core use during its second nesting attempt, although it was closer to its initial core use area than some of the movements displayed by the other birds discussed above.
> >
> > Thanks in advance for any guidance you all can provide!
> >
> > Best,
> > Tyler
> >
> >

messages.subject_clean: iRSF with multiple categorial variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

The effective sample size should decrease with every predictor that you include in the model. If you include too many unsupported parameters, then it can become too small. If you have two categorical variables, with 5 categories each, then that's 8 parameters added. You have to consider if your data can support that many parameters (e.g., does AIC go down? are the parameter estimates significant?). With categorical variables you often have to consider merging categories.

If your AIC is going down, your parameter estimates are significantly non-zero, and yet your effective sample size is also vanishing, then that would be more surprising to me - let me know if that's the case.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: RSFs
messages.subject_clean: RSFs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

After lengthy discussions with my project collaborators about the best approach for our analysis given the limitations of our data (e.g. small sample sizes for some individuals), we have decided to go with a more traditional approach to the RSF analysis (i.e used-available approach using logistic regression modelling) rather than rsf.fit(), whilst being aware of the drawbacks of doing so.

We have decided to take this approach for a couple of reasons:
i) Retain flexibility in our approach: This will allow us to use just random intercept only models if we need to so we can assess all data, BUT if sample sizes allow, we can also try running random slope models to account for individual variability. We have concerns over the low numbers of kill or bed sites for some individuals and don't want our sample size of individual animals to be reduced by only modelling RSFs individually in rsf.fit().
ii) Assessing habitat selection relative to entire home range rather just a small section of the home range in the case of bed and kill site habitat selection: As you pointed out previously, for assessing kill or bed site selection we would need to generate separate UDs per set of kill or bed sites per individual animal, but given this can be as few as 5 to 10 kill or bed sites for some animals, the UD created will not cover the entire home range and will therefore not be assessing habitat selection of kill or bed sites relative to the entire home range, but instead just a small fraction of it. Additionally, we want to compare selection across the home range using all tracking data vs bed sites vs kill sites. Ultimately we we want to predict kill and bed site habitat across the landscape and determine the proportion of these areas within each individual's home range.

Given we are going with a more traditional approach, we are going to generate a certain number available points per used point (somewhere in the range of 10-100 as per Muff et al. 2019. We may also do some type of sensitivity analysis to determine threshold) my questions are:

1. Would it be suitable to use the weights generated in akde(), that are assigned to each location, in subsequent logistic regression models using all the tracking data within a traditional used-available approach? Will the weights still be accounting for autocorrelation/pseudoreplication and irregularities in fix rates and fix success, OR are they only valid with a suitable movement model? Or by using a traditional approach will there be no movement model and locations will be considered to be IID and the weights are still useful?
Note: Weights aren't a concern for the kill and bed sites because we can consider these independent locations, however we want to generate RSFs for all the location/tracking data so we can compare how habitat selection compares between all data vs kill sites vs bed sites, relative to what is available in the individual's home range.

2. Would using these weights mean we wouldn't need to assign an arbitrary large weight to available points (e.g. 1000 or more) as described in Muff et al. 2019, or would it be wise to do both using the traditional used-available logistic regression approach?

3. Do the weights generated and assigned by akde() also account for the error (e.g. DOP) associated with each GPS location/fix?

4. Fix success varies between 15% to 97% across individuals, with 66 of 76 animals with a fix success rate of <80%. However, it appears that assigning of weights using akde() deals with this issue and I don't need to go down the path of assessing potential habitat-biased fix success (e.g. 1/Pfix as per Frair et al. 2010), given Alston et al. 2022 states: "As an additional benefit, likelihood weights can also account for sampling biases that arise from irregular sampling. Such bias can occur, for example, when covariates are over- or under-sampled, such as when environmental covariates are associated with differential probability of successful triangulation of animal locations (Fleming et al., 2018 <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025#mee314025-bib-0026>; Frair et al., 2010 <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025#mee314025-bib-0028>; Lewis et al., 2007 <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025#mee314025-bib-0042>)." Is this because the irregular, or more temporally isolated fixes, are given greater weight because they are less correlated with other fixes, and hence it accounts for sampling irregularities due to collar failure or habitat effects, etc.?

Regards,
Luke

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke,

i. Random intercepts don't really do anything: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2656.13087
Random slopes are worth trying if you can't get anything out of the individual RSFs but want to try to get something out of the population. You can do this to a degree with mean(rsf.fit()), if the individual likelihoods increase on the order of 1 by including the parameter of interest, but a random-slope model is slightly more permissive, and could potentially tease out population-level significance from many individuals with weaker individual-level support (the weaker the support, the more individuals you would need). But not accounting for the autocorrelation is also going to return false positives, so if you don't address that, then you might think you are getting something out but are just getting noise.

ii. I don't see the issue, but maybe I'm not fully understand what you are doing. The distribution of kill/bet sites is what it is. Either the data are representative of that distribution or the sample is biased, and if its the latter, then you would have to adjust for that in some other way in the model.

Definitely do a sensitivity analysis on the parameter estimates by doubling the number of available points until convergence.

1. It depends on how the weights enter into the model - they need to weight the log-likelihood itself. If you can give me a reference, then I can tell you. But, in principle, yes.

2. You need both, because you are using glm as a round-about way of approximating an inhomogeneous Poisson point process model. The weights used in rsf.fit() don't need to include that because ctmm is directly evaluating an inhomogeneous Poisson point process model.

3. Not yet, but I'm about to put in support for that.

4. Yes.

Best,
Chris

> Hi Chris,
>
> After lengthy discussions with my project collaborators about the best approach for our analysis given the limitations of our data (e.g. small sample sizes for some individuals), we have decided to go with a more traditional approach to the RSF analysis (i.e used-available approach using logistic regression modelling) rather than rsf.fit(), whilst being aware of the drawbacks of doing so.
>
> We have decided to take this approach for a couple of reasons:
> i) Retain flexibility in our approach: This will allow us to use just random intercept only models if we need to so we can assess all data, BUT if sample sizes allow, we can also try running random slope models to account for individual variability. We have concerns over the low numbers of kill or bed sites for some individuals and don't want our sample size of individual animals to be reduced by only modelling RSFs individually in rsf.fit().
> ii) Assessing habitat selection relative to entire home range rather just a small section of the home range in the case of bed and kill site habitat selection: As you pointed out previously, for assessing kill or bed site selection we would need to generate separate UDs per set of kill or bed sites per individual animal, but given this can be as few as 5 to 10 kill or bed sites for some animals, the UD created will not cover the entire home range and will therefore not be assessing habitat selection of kill or bed sites relative to the entire home range, but instead just a small fraction of it. Additionally, we want to compare selection across the home range using all tracking data vs bed sites vs kill sites. Ultimately we we want to predict kill and bed site habitat across the landscape and determine the proportion of these areas within each individual's home range.
>
>
> Given we are going with a more traditional approach, we are going to generate a certain number available points per used point (somewhere in the range of 10-100 as per Muff et al. 2019. We may also do some type of sensitivity analysis to determine threshold) my questions are:

Or by using a traditional approach will there be no movement model and locations will be considered to be IID and the weights are still useful?
> Note: Weights aren't a concern for the kill and bed sites because we can consider these independent locations, however we want to generate RSFs for all the location/tracking data so we can compare how habitat selection compares between all data vs kill sites vs bed sites, relative to what is available in the individual's home range.
>
> 2. Would using these weights mean we wouldn't need to assign an arbitrary large weight to available points (e.g. 1000 or more) as described in Muff et al. 2019, or would it be wise to do both using the traditional used-available logistic regression approach?

>
> 4. Fix success varies between 15% to 97% across individuals, with 66 of 76 animals with a fix success rate of <80%. However, it appears that assigning of weights using akde() deals with this issue and I don't need to go down the path of assessing potential habitat-biased fix success (e.g. 1/Pfix as per Frair et al. 2010), given Alston et al. 2022 states: "As an additional benefit, likelihood weights can also account for sampling biases that arise from irregular sampling. Such bias can occur, for example, when covariates are over- or under-sampled, such as when environmental covariates are associated with differential probability of successful triangulation of animal locations (Fleming et al., 2018 <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025#mee314025-bib-0026>; Frair et al., 2010 <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025#mee314025-bib-0028>; Lewis et al., 2007 <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025#mee314025-bib-0042>)." Is this because the irregular, or more temporally isolated fixes, are given greater weight because they are less correlated with other fixes, and hence it accounts for sampling irregularities due to collar failure or habitat effects, etc.?
>
> Regards,
> Luke

Hi Chris, I'm hoping you can help me out with a couple of things.
The first: I have telemetry tracking data from sharks using high density arrays, that render positions accurate to a few meters, with positions every couple minutes or so.
If I run the animals individually, following the methods described in the paper, I can run ADKEs (weighted or not) without a problem.
However, when I follow the vignette to run them as a batch in parallel, it will not run the WAKDEs for my data. It will do it just fine for the example Buffalo data, but for my data, R never stops (at least after 2.5 days) trying to run it. The unweighted ADKE in parallel works just fine. Can you think of any reasons this may be?

The second issue: I'm trying to look at Conditional Distribution of Encounters.
the first attempt at using the cde function yielded the following response

`Error in cde(ADKES[c("2020-13","2020-15")]) : could not find function cde.

So i looked up the source code for the function, ran that separately, then tried again.
This time it returned the error: `Error in check.projection(UD) : could not find function "check.projection".
I also tried CDE<- stmm::cde(ADKES[c("2020-13","2020-15")], but got the error `Error: 'cde' is not an exported object from namespace:ctmm'

Again, any ideas or pointers would be greatly appreciated.
Cheers,

James

Hi James,

If the individuals have ranges with vastly different scales, then you can run out of memory (or take forever calculating with virtual memory) trying to put everything on a high resolution grid. I recently added a dr.fn argument to the grid argument of akde() that you can quickly use to automate a coarser resolution like akde(...,grid=list(dr.fn=max)) which will take the maximum individual cell size, whereas the default will take the minimum individual cell size. Please see if that works.

Best,
Chris

> Random slopes are worth trying if you can't get anything out of the individual RSFs but want to try to get something out of the population. You can do this to a degree with mean(rsf.fit()), if the individual likelihoods increase on the order of 1 by including the parameter of interest, but a random-slope model is slightly more permissive, and could potentially tease out population-level significance from many individuals with weaker individual-level support (the weaker the support, the more individuals you would need). But not accounting for the autocorrelation is also going to return false positives, so if you don't address that, then you might think you are getting something out but are just getting noise.
>
> ii. I don't see the issue, but maybe I'm not fully understand what you are doing. The distribution of kill/bet sites is what it is. Either the data are representative of that distribution or the sample is biased, and if its the latter, then you would have to adjust for that in some other way in the model.
>

>
> 1. It depends on how the weights enter into the model - they need to weight the log-likelihood itself. If you can give me a reference, then I can tell you. But, in principle, yes.
>
> 2. You need both, because you are using glm as a round-about way of approximating an inhomogeneous Poisson point process model. The weights used in rsf.fit() don't need to include that because ctmm is directly evaluating an inhomogeneous Poisson point process model.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > We are wanting to assess the influence of study area/population level factors (including the presence or not of wolves, bears, and/or puma hunting by humans) on the selection of critical habitat characteristics (specifically feeding/kill sites and bed sites) of pumas. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Given the presence of bears and hunting are seasonal, it would seem prudent that we create seasonal RSFs. Below is a potential workflow:

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Habitat selection per seasonal home range:

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. all locations
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. all kill sites
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. all bed sites

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 9. summer bed sites
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Questions:

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. If I want to assess seasonal habitat selection, do I need to first create a seasonal akde (i.e. Winter kill site selection should only be assessed relative to winter akde, not the entire akde across all seasons)?
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >

> > Hi Luke,

> > i. Random intercepts don't really do anything: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2656.13087
> > Random slopes are worth trying if you can't get anything out of the individual RSFs but want to try to get something out of the population. You can do this to a degree with mean(rsf.fit()), if the individual likelihoods increase on the order of 1 by including the parameter of interest, but a random-slope model is slightly more permissive, and could potentially tease out population-level significance from many individuals with weaker individual-level support (the weaker the support, the more individuals you would need). But not accounting for the autocorrelation is also going to return false positives, so if you don't address that, then you might think you are getting something out but are just getting noise.
> >
> > ii. I don't see the issue, but maybe I'm not fully understand what you are doing. The distribution of kill/bet sites is what it is. Either the data are representative of that distribution or the sample is biased, and if its the latter, then you would have to adjust for that in some other way in the model.
> >
> > Definitely do a sensitivity analysis on the parameter estimates by doubling the number of available points until convergence.
> >
> > 1. It depends on how the weights enter into the model - they need to weight the log-likelihood itself. If you can give me a reference, then I can tell you. But, in principle, yes.
> >
> > 2. You need both, because you are using glm as a round-about way of approximating an inhomogeneous Poisson point process model. The weights used in rsf.fit() don't need to include that because ctmm is directly evaluating an inhomogeneous Poisson point process model.
> >
> > 3. Not yet, but I'm about to put in support for that.
> >

We have concerns over the low numbers of kill or bed sites for some individuals and don't want our sample size of individual animals to be reduced by only modelling RSFs individually in rsf.fit().
> > > ii) Assessing habitat selection relative to entire home range rather just a small section of the home range in the case of bed and kill site habitat selection: As you pointed out previously, for assessing kill or bed site selection we would need to generate separate UDs per set of kill or bed sites per individual animal, but given this can be as few as 5 to 10 kill or bed sites for some animals, the UD created will not cover the entire home range and will therefore not be assessing habitat selection of kill or bed sites relative to the entire home range, but instead just a small fraction of it. Additionally, we want to compare selection across the home range using all tracking data vs bed sites vs kill sites. Ultimately we we want to predict kill and bed site habitat across the landscape and determine the proportion of these areas within each individual's home range.
> > >
> > >
> > > Given we are going with a more traditional approach, we are going to generate a certain number available points per used point (somewhere in the range of 10-100 as per Muff et al. 2019. We may also do some type of sensitivity analysis to determine threshold) my questions are:

> > > 1. Would it be suitable to use the weights generated in akde(), that are assigned to each location, in subsequent logistic regression models using all the tracking data within a traditional used-available approach? Will the weights still be accounting for autocorrelation/pseudoreplication and irregularities in fix rates and fix success, OR are they only valid with a suitable movement model? Or by using a traditional approach will there be no movement model and locations will be considered to be IID and the weights are still useful?
> > > Note: Weights aren't a concern for the kill and bed sites because we can consider these independent locations, however we want to generate RSFs for all the location/tracking data so we can compare how habitat selection compares between all data vs kill sites vs bed sites, relative to what is available in the individual's home range.
> > >
> > > 2. Would using these weights mean we wouldn't need to assign an arbitrary large weight to available points (e.g. 1000 or more) as described in Muff et al. 2019, or would it be wise to do both using the traditional used-available logistic regression approach?

However, it appears that assigning of weights using akde() deals with this issue and I don't need to go down the path of assessing potential habitat-biased fix success (e.g. 1/Pfix as per Frair et al. 2010), given Alston et al. 2022 states: "As an additional benefit, likelihood weights can also account for sampling biases that arise from irregular sampling. Is this because the irregular, or more temporally isolated fixes, are given greater weight because they are less correlated with other fixes, and hence it accounts for sampling irregularities due to collar failure or habitat effects, etc.?

> > > Regards,
> > > Luke

You can do this to a degree with mean(rsf.fit()), if the individual likelihoods increase on the order of 1 by including the parameter of interest, but a random-slope model is slightly more permissive, and could potentially tease out population-level significance from many individuals with weaker individual-level support (the weaker the support, the more individuals you would need). > > > > Hi Chris,

> > > > After lengthy discussions with my project collaborators about the best approach for our analysis given the limitations of our data (e.g. small sample sizes for some individuals), we have decided to go with a more traditional approach to the RSF analysis (i.e used-available approach using logistic regression modelling) rather than rsf.fit(), whilst being aware of the drawbacks of doing so.
> > > >
> > > > We have decided to take this approach for a couple of reasons:
> > > > i) Retain flexibility in our approach: This will allow us to use just random intercept only models if we need to so we can assess all data, BUT if sample sizes allow, we can also try running random slope models to account for individual variability. We have concerns over the low numbers of kill or bed sites for some individuals and don't want our sample size of individual animals to be reduced by only modelling RSFs individually in rsf.fit().
> > > > ii) Assessing habitat selection relative to entire home range rather just a small section of the home range in the case of bed and kill site habitat selection: As you pointed out previously, for assessing kill or bed site selection we would need to generate separate UDs per set of kill or bed sites per individual animal, but given this can be as few as 5 to 10 kill or bed sites for some animals, the UD created will not cover the entire home range and will therefore not be assessing habitat selection of kill or bed sites relative to the entire home range, but instead just a small fraction of it. Additionally, we want to compare selection across the home range using all tracking data vs bed sites vs kill sites. Ultimately we we want to predict kill and bed site habitat across the landscape and determine the proportion of these areas within each individual's home range.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Given we are going with a more traditional approach, we are going to generate a certain number available points per used point (somewhere in the range of 10-100 as per Muff et al. 2019. We may also do some type of sensitivity analysis to determine threshold) my questions are:
> > > >
> > > > 1. Would it be suitable to use the weights generated in akde(), that are assigned to each location, in subsequent logistic regression models using all the tracking data within a traditional used-available approach? Will the weights still be accounting for autocorrelation/pseudoreplication and irregularities in fix rates and fix success, OR are they only valid with a suitable movement model? Or by using a traditional approach will there be no movement model and locations will be considered to be IID and the weights are still useful?
> > > > Note: Weights aren't a concern for the kill and bed sites because we can consider these independent locations, however we want to generate RSFs for all the location/tracking data so we can compare how habitat selection compares between all data vs kill sites vs bed sites, relative to what is available in the individual's home range.
> > > >
> > > > 2. Would using these weights mean we wouldn't need to assign an arbitrary large weight to available points (e.g. 1000 or more) as described in Muff et al. 2019, or would it be wise to do both using the traditional used-available logistic regression approach?
> > > >
> > > > 3. Do the weights generated and assigned by akde() also account for the error (e.g. DOP) associated with each GPS location/fix?
> > > >
> > > > 4. Fix success varies between 15% to 97% across individuals, with 66 of 76 animals with a fix success rate of <80%. However, it appears that assigning of weights using akde() deals with this issue and I don't need to go down the path of assessing potential habitat-biased fix success (e.g. 1/Pfix as per Frair et al. 2010), given Alston et al. 2022 states: "As an additional benefit, likelihood weights can also account for sampling biases that arise from irregular sampling. Such bias can occur, for example, when covariates are over- or under-sampled, such as when environmental covariates are associated with differential probability of successful triangulation of animal locations (Fleming et al., 2018 <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025#mee314025-bib-0026>; Frair et al., 2010 <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025#mee314025-bib-0028>; Lewis et al., 2007 <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025#mee314025-bib-0042>)." Is this because the irregular, or more temporally isolated fixes, are given greater weight because they are less correlated with other fixes, and hence it accounts for sampling irregularities due to collar failure or habitat effects, etc.?

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I just noticed that some locations fall outside the 95% estimate UD (i.e. home range polygon). I am just trying to inform my approach for assessing available vs used points and I was wondering, does rsf.fit() only sample available space within the UD but compares against all tracking location data to assess selection, even if some locations from the tracking data fall outside the UD?

Cheers,
Luke.

> > > > > ii) Assessing habitat selection relative to entire home range rather just a small section of the home range in the case of bed and kill site habitat selection: As you pointed out previously, for assessing kill or bed site selection we would need to generate separate UDs per set of kill or bed sites per individual animal, but given this can be as few as 5 to 10 kill or bed sites for some animals, the UD created will not cover the entire home range and will therefore not be assessing habitat selection of kill or bed sites relative to the entire home range, but instead just a small fraction of it. messages.body_plain:
hi Chris,

I've been running exploratory analyses on movements of male elephants of dispersal age, and I'm not having much luck with movement models (they just run and run in the processor).

Collars should fix every hour, with 25,000-39,000 fixes per individual (collars have been on for several years to track dispersal strategies). I've successfully plotted variograms and went to select best-fit movement models with the intention of fitting AKDE HR estimates. Previously I had got through 4 of my 8 males with 15-60 minutes processing time, but one male ran overnight without a result, and if I set verbose = TRUE none of the models now finish running. Fitting with pHREML never finishes either.

I'm wondering if a sampling interval anomaly I spotted might be the reason, and if not whether my sample sizes are problematic. The intention was to run all data together, and then break down by season, dispersal stage and male age.

Thanks for any help

Vicki

*******

library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ctmm)
EReles <- st_read("Elephants.gpkg")
ctmmformat <- subset(EReles, select = c(extra__subject__name, fixtime))
rm(EReles)

ctmmformat <- ctmmformat %>% mutate(lon = st_coordinates(.)[,1],
                                     lat = st_coordinates(.)[,2]) %>%
        st_drop_geometry() %>%
        rename("ID" = "extra__subject__name", "timestamp" = "fixtime",
               "longitude" = "lon", "latitude" = "lat")

# >>> this generates ID as chr, timestamp as POSIXct, longitude and latitude as numbers.

#make ele-by-ele format

ESP <- filter(ctmmformat, ID== c("Esposito"))
PAK <- filter(ctmmformat, ID== c("Pakwach"))

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke,

By default, rsf.fit() does not sample from coverage areas of the UD.  By default, rsf.fit() estimates an integrated RSF (iRSF) where the availability parameters are estimated with the resource-selection parameters, analogous to integrated SSFs. You can see what that model looks like with agde().

Best,
Chris

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vicki,

Yes, those warnings are there for a reason. How far does an elephant tend to travel in 6 seconds compared to the GPS error?
If you leave the data as-is and run a default model without location error modeled, then the models will all fit very poorly and could take a very long time to fit due to a multi-modal likelihood function.
If you thin the data down to 15-60 minutes where you don't need a location-error model, then that shouldn't be an issue.
If you keep all of the data and supply a location-error model, then the model can then fit that data much better, but you will be fitting many more parameters with a higher-dimensional Kalman filter, so this will be about 10× slower than 2.
In either case, the algorithms are O(n) and so processing 40,000 locations will take about 10× longer to compute than 4,000 locations.
In either case, trace=3 in ctmm.select() will give you a progress bar.
You should be able to trivially parallelize computation over multiple individuals with foreach, but then you can't see individual progress.
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,

To follow up on Chris' point--if you are going to perform a conventional RSF, we would strongly recommend that you use the 100% contour (e.g., a 100% MCP) rather than a 95% contour. You don't want the animal to have "used" points that you label as unavailable--it is philosophically problematic and causes some statistical issues as well. That is one reason we prefer the "integrated" approach Chris installed as the default option in rsf.fit().

Jesse

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I'm very new to home range analyses so I hope this isn't an obvious question. I have a telemetry dataset of 117 lizards. Lizards were tracked 1-2x/day during a ~3 month season each year. A new set of ~30-40 lizards was tracked each year for 3 years. I'm trying to compare the average 95% UD of the population across years. I think I've done everything right– followed the first half of example code at the end of the meta function description. However, although the code should have calculated the AKDEs on a consistent grid, I'm still finding my bandwidths are different (0.5<h<0.7) for each individual when I look at the output dataset.

1) Is it appropriate to compare across years given these slightly different bandwidths? Are there further analyses you recommend to ensure a fair comparison?
2) I didn't thin my original dataset at all, so there are some individuals with <10 observations (due to slipped collars) and some with 70 observations (collared the entire season). From what I understand, this should be okay for AKDEs. Is that correct or would you recommend excluding lizards below a threshold number of resightings?

Thank you for any feedback,
Emme

Hi Emme,
Yes, and I realize that there are numerous papers published in wildlife and ecology journals that discuss averaging the bandwidth across individuals, but I've never seen any reference to the statistics literature on KDE to justify this. The individual AKDE bandwidths are optimized to minimize bias and variance, then in AKDEc there is an additional bias reduction, and finally in all comparisons made in ctmm the uncertainties are propagated. Fixing the bandwidth will increase the bias and variance by an unknown amount, and that bias will not necessarily be consistent across individuals, because it depends on both the sampling schedule and the movement characteristics. I think the old arguments for standardizing the sampling schedules make sense with older analyses, but standardizing the bandwidths will under-smooth some individuals while over-smoothing others. I don't see how introducing a mix of positive and negative biases could possibly help anything.
https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13270
https://github.com/ctmm-initiative/ctmmlearn/blob/main/ctmm_effective_sample_sizes.R
The default estimates are pretty good down to effective sample sizes of 4-5, and ctmm.boot() can get you down to 2-3. Since your small-DOF individuals are at random (slipped collars), then it should be safe to throw out the bad estimates to reduce negative bias. [In other cases where all individuals are sampled similarly and the small-DOF individuals correspond to larger movements, throwing out the worst estimates could actually increase the negative bias.]
Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Chris and Jesse for that info and advice.

I had wondered if I needed to instead use MCP in this instance, so thank you for confirming Jesse!

Just to clarify why we have decided to go with a traditional RSF approach; it is because we have concerns over model fitting when sample sizes are small for the number of kill and bed sites per individual. We didn't want to lose data because models wouldn't fit for some individuals. For this reason we decided to pool all data together to run our various RSFs which will then allow us to model random intercepts and slopes when analyzing habitat selection for kill and bed site data. This allows us to keep the approach the same when using all the tracking data to create RSFs and when just assessing the bed and kill site data.

I am convinced that the approach your team has developed is the most robust method to use for estimating home ranges and performing RSFs, BUT given our modelling concerns for the small sample sizes for bed and kill sites, we need to resort to a more traditional and slightly less robust approach where we can pool the data. Fortunately, we can Frankenstein our approach somewhat by using the weights generated by akde() to account for autocorrelation, etc. in our models!! We will also be using home ranges from akde() for a later stage of the analysis, so the learnings from this process have not been in vain! :)

Many thanks for all the help and advice!

Regards,
Luke

messages.subject_clean: ctmm.boot error and increasing computational efficiency
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Big thanks to this group for all of the great questions and information, particularly Chris for your endless help and responsiveness.

I am attempting to calculate AKDEs for several individuals within a population, and hoping to calculate a PKDE as well. Similar to the gazelles in the Fleming et al 2019 supplement, the species I’m working with has very few range crossings (N << n), some with DOFs of 5-8, while others have DOFs of 2-4. Total observations (GPS fixes) range from ~600-4,000. For those individuals with DOFs <5 I am attempting to use ctmm.boot to run the parametric bootstrap; however, I have a few questions:

Firstly, I installed the latest development version of ctmm from the Git repository, and when I run ctmm.boot(telemetry, fit[[1]], iterate = TRUE, trace = TRUE) I receive the following error:

Error in !POS : invalid argument type.

I uninstalled this version and reinstalled the package from CRAN, and ran the same code without error. I repeated this process on two computers with the same results, so it seems there may be an issue with ctmm.boot in the most recent version (?) Has anyone else encountered this?

Secondly, I understand the function is computationally expensive. It has been running for about 6 days for one individual with ~2500 observations. It’s still only at 83% percent and likely needs to go through additional iterations. In Fleming et al 2019, they state 'relative error <<5% will become computationally wasteful', whereas I believe the default is 1%. Should I change this to 5%? Alternatively, given the computational cost, would it be advisable to switch iterate = FALSE and/or thin my data? Not sure if that would reduce computation time, but, again, the animals cross their range on a seasonal basis, and I have 4hr fix rates, which seems like overkill given the range crossing frequency.

Any insights would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you,

Tyler

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tyler,

If you can please send me a minimal working example that can replicate that error, then I can take a look at it. I just added a feature to ctmm.boot so that you can safely increase the error argument without the variance estimates becoming noisy. That probably introduced a bug.

That statement from Fleming et al. (2019) is explaining that its wasteful to set the numerical error target (the error argument) to be much lower than the relative bias of O(1/DOF^3) that the bootstrapped pHREML estimate can obtain.

error=0.05 will be 25 times faster than the default of error=0.01. iterate=FALSE will also be a couple of times faster. Sampling intervals much smaller than the range crossing timescale are going to give you diminishing returns in the home-range estimation. Finally, I will add that ctmm.boot is one of the functions in ctmm that is parallelized with the cores argument. If you have 8 cores, then you can turn that up to run 8 times faster, as bootstrapping is embarrassingly parallelizable.

Best,
Chris

On Friday, October 27, 2023 at 1:19:45 PM UTC-7 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Tyler,
>
> If you can please send me a minimal working example that can replicate that error, then I can take a look at it. I just added a feature to ctmm.boot so that you can safely increase the error argument without the variance estimates becoming noisy. That probably introduced a bug.
>
> That statement from Fleming et al. (2019) is explaining that its wasteful to set the numerical error target (the error argument) to be much lower than the relative bias of O(1/DOF^3) that the bootstrapped pHREML estimate can obtain.
>
> error=0.05 will be 25 times faster than the default of error=0.01. iterate=FALSE will also be a couple of times faster. Sampling intervals much smaller than the range crossing timescale are going to give you diminishing returns in the home-range estimation. Finally, I will add that ctmm.boot is one of the functions in ctmm that is parallelized with the cores argument. If you have 8 cores, then you can turn that up to run 8 times faster, as bootstrapping is embarrassingly parallelizable.
>
> Best,
> Chris
>
> On Friday, October 27, 2023 at 11:52:17 AM UTC-4 Tyler wrote:
> >
